source.title: Gi and Pal Scores: Deep Neural Network Generalization Statistics
source.authors: Yair Schiff; Brian Quanz; Payel Das; Pin-Yu Chen

record.tranche_reason: Measures whether interpolation-perturbation scores predict generalization gaps, using a different perturbation and prediction measure from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports task-level average CMI scores for Gi and Pal measures and comparators. Its scores use interpolation of training inputs or representations; it does not measure the weight perturbations, architecture comparisons, or other interventions specified in V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates its own interpolation-response statistics as predictors of generalization gaps. It does not test any V1–V8 intervention or relationship. In particular, input and representation interpolation do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled weight sharpness. Citing Jiang et al. does not establish a test or use of that finding.
record.authors_conclusion: The record largely captures the conclusion: Gi and Pal scores applied to linear interpolation perform strongly at predicting gaps in this corpus. The authors also propose them as measures of transformation invariance, while leaving further validation and applications of that interpretation to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses input or representation interpolation and average CMI scores to predict gaps; the claim versions specify other interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Task, architecture, interpolation type (inter-class or intra-class), and perturbation depth (input or shallowest layer) vary across reported results.

fits_no_version.finding: Interpolation-response Gi and Pal statistics predict generalization gaps with task- and depth-dependent performance. Their best variants exceed DBI*Mixup on four of eight tasks, but not on CINIC-10 or Oxford Flowers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Statistics summarizing accuracy across input or representation interpolation magnitudes can predict generalization gaps in pretrained image classifiers.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented as a RobustML workshop paper at ICLR 2021
record.problems: The reported CMI values are task averages across networks; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper states that each network attains nearly perfect training accuracy, but this study does not test the specific interventions in V1–V8.
record.rows_left_out: Four Table 1 entries for Fashion MNIST VGG intra-class mixup (Gi and Pal, l=0 and l=1) omitted to meet the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same training recipe; chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test-error changes when width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and the contribution of learned or imposed local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, weight-decay changes, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and remedies through training-recipe changes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data sizes, strengths, and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All 60 extracted numerical values and task assignments match Table 1. These are CMI evaluations of prediction methods, not direct effect sizes for any claim version, so they should remain outside the claim-evidence rows. Asterisks indicate that the task's best mixup-based measure exceeds DBI*Mixup; they are not significance markers. The four omitted Fashion MNIST entries are declared in rows_left_out and do not bear on V1–V8. Neither nearly perfect natural-label training accuracy nor variation across convolutional architectures supplies the missing comparisons for V1–V3.

versions.untested_parts: Magnitude-aware weight perturbations and comparisons to norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.
